aiPrompt.systemPrompt: You are a master middle school math teacher.
aiPrompt.mainPrompt: Below is a student's mathematics document, as a text summary, a picture, or both. Either may be absent. Evaluate and categorize it.
aiPrompt.categorizationDescription: Categorize the document based on its content and the general proportional reasoning curriculum found in middle grades mathematics.
aiPrompt.keyIndicatorsPrompt: Return exactly one item: a single sentence of at most 30 words, written to the student as "you", saying why this category fits by naming one specific thing in their document - a number, ratio, label, table column, or phrase they actually wrote. Do not restate the problem, summarize the document as a whole, or explain the mathematics in general.

aiUnitSummary.overview: Flip, Spin, Slide, and Stretch is a grade 8 geometry unit that rebuilds congruence and similarity on transformations. Investigation 1 introduces reflections, translations and rotations one at a time, each through the relationship between a point, its image and the defining object — the mirror line, the translation vector, the centre of rotation — and then asks students to identify which transformation produced a given image and what combinations of two can achieve. Investigation 2 uses that to define congruence: two figures are congruent when a sequence of these transformations carries one onto the other, which leads into minimum conditions for triangle congruence and into transformation arguments for the parallel-line angle relationships and the 180° triangle sum. Investigation 3 puts the transformations on a coordinate grid and derives rules of the form (x, y) → (■, ■) for each. Investigation 4 adds dilation, defines similarity as a dilation combined with congruence transformations, and returns to similar triangles and indirect measurement.

entries.priorKnowledge: From Shapes and Designs: properties of polygons, minimum conditions determining a unique triangle, and congruence as same shape and size. From Stretching and Shrinking: scale drawings, similar figures and scale factor, and the Wump characters used as a running context. Students should be able to work on a coordinate grid, though grid rules come later in this unit.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces reflection as the first transformation. Students examine a quadrilateral and its image across a line and are asked what they notice, whether the two have the same size and shape, and what the relationship is between a point and its image with respect to the reflection line — the answer, that the line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them, being the result the whole investigation rests on. The What If section reverses the question: given a pentagon and its image but no line, students find the line of reflection. They then draw an image without a mirror, folding or tracing, using only the point-to-image relationship, which tests whether they have the property rather than a procedure.
entries.approachGuidance: Students notice and describe the relationship before it is named, and find images without tracing. Support the property they articulate rather than supplying a construction.

entries.priorKnowledge: Reflection as a transformation, and the perpendicular relationship between a point, its image and the mirror line; congruence as same shape and size; drawing images from a defining relationship rather than by tracing.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces translation as a slide, motivated by wallpaper whose repeated sailboat pattern looks unchanged when the paper is slid. Students examine Mug's hat and its images under two different translations and describe the relationship between a point, its image and the translation line — each point moving the same distance in the same direction. The What If section has them translate the hat along a given segment, then find the translation that puts the hat on Mug's head and the one that returns it, which makes the inverse explicit. A final situation has students identify a translation line and its length from a figure and its image.
entries.approachGuidance: Students describe the pattern they observe before it is formalised. Support their description of the relationship rather than naming a vector.

entries.priorKnowledge: Reflections and translations, and the point-to-image relationship that defines each; congruence; angle measure in degrees and the idea of a turn from Shapes and Designs; drawing an image from a defining relationship.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces rotation about a centre. A flag is rotated about a point C and students describe what they notice, compare original and image, work out the angle of rotation, and state the relationship between a point, its image and the centre — each point staying the same distance from the centre and turning through the same angle. The What If section has students carry out rotations of a flag about one of its own vertices, then considers Marti's claim that a 180° rotation is the same as a reflection, which is false in general and worth the argument. A final situation reverses the problem: given two rotations of a triangle, find the centre.
entries.approachGuidance: Marti's claim invites a counterexample rather than a verdict handed down. Support students testing it rather than ruling on it.

entries.priorKnowledge: Reflections, translations and rotations, and for each the relationship between a point, its image and the defining line or centre; congruence as same shape and size; finding a mirror line, a translation line or a centre from a figure and its image.
entries.problemDigest: Asks students to work backwards from an image to the transformation that produced it. A trapezoid is shown moved three ways, and for each students identify the transformation and give its specifics — the reflection line, the direction and distance of the translation, or the angle and centre of the rotation — and compare the trapezoid with its image. The What If section tabulates what each transformation preserves, then composes two transformations and asks how the final image relates to the original and whether a single transformation could replace the pair; kaleidoscope designs are then analysed as repeated transformations. The closing question asks what changes and what does not, including for parallel lines and angles.
entries.approachGuidance: More than one sequence of transformations can produce the same image, and composing them is open-ended. Accept any sequence a student can justify.

entries.priorKnowledge: The three congruence transformations and what each preserves; composing two transformations; identifying a transformation from a figure and its image; congruence as same shape and size; corresponding parts of figures.
entries.problemDigest: Defines congruence in terms of transformations: one figure is congruent to another if a sequence of reflections, translations and rotations carries the first onto the second. Students apply this to pairs of triangles, deciding which pairs are congruent and demonstrating it by giving an actual sequence of transformations rather than by comparing measurements, and listing the corresponding vertices when they are. Pairs that are not congruent must also be argued. This is the pivot of the unit — congruence stops being a checklist of equal sides and angles and becomes a question of whether one figure can be moved onto another.
entries.approachGuidance: Several different sequences will map one triangle onto another. Support any sequence that works rather than a canonical one.

entries.priorKnowledge: Congruence as the existence of a sequence of transformations carrying one figure onto another; that congruent figures have equal corresponding sides and angles; tick and arc notation for marking congruent parts; from Shapes and Designs, which sets of conditions determine a unique triangle.
entries.problemDigest: Asks how little information is enough to force congruence. Students play a game in which one partner must give the minimum set of directions for the other to draw a congruent figure, then describe the strategies that worked and what the minimal clues were. The What If section collects a class's claims about minimum conditions for two triangles to be congruent and asks students to argue for each or produce a counterexample — so the familiar side-and-angle criteria are established by testing rather than stated. The closing question asks directly for the least information about sides and angles that guarantees congruence.
entries.approachGuidance: Students propose conditions and test them, and a counterexample is as valuable as a proof. Support the testing rather than confirming the standard criteria.

entries.priorKnowledge: Congruence by transformation; the three congruence transformations and what each preserves; from Shapes and Designs, parallel lines, transversals, and the vertical, supplementary and corresponding angle relationships, and that a triangle's angles sum to 180°.
entries.problemDigest: Uses transformations to explain results previously found by measurement. Two parallel lines cut by a transversal give eight angles, and students examine conjectures about using transformations to show that angles 1, 3, 5 and 7 are congruent and likewise the other four — a translation along the transversal carrying one intersection onto the other, or a rotation about a midpoint. For each conjecture students say whether the method works and why, with diagrams. The What If section then has students supply the reasons for each step of a transformation argument that a triangle's angles sum to 180°, turning a measured result into a justified one.
entries.approachGuidance: Several transformation arguments work for each result and students justify rather than compute. Support the argument a student is constructing.

entries.priorKnowledge: Translations and the relationship between a point, its image and the translation line; plotting and reading coordinates in four quadrants; from Stretching and Shrinking, coordinate rules used to make the Wump characters; congruence by transformation.
entries.problemDigest: Puts translation on the coordinate grid and asks for a rule. Four Mug figures are shown, and students write the coordinate rule (x, y) → (■, ■) carrying the first to each of the others, then describe the pattern — a constant added to each coordinate. The What If section tests Nina's claim that a segment and its translated image are parallel, asking both whether she is right in the instance and whether the coordinate rule guarantees it in general. Students then write the rule for a translation of 5 units horizontally and 2 vertically, and identify which part of the rule is what keeps the size and shape unchanged, connecting the algebra back to the geometry.
entries.approachGuidance: Students find the rule from the pattern in the coordinates. Let the generalisation come from their examples rather than stating the rule.

entries.priorKnowledge: Reflections and the perpendicular relationship defining them; coordinate rules for translations and how the rule preserves size and shape; plotting points in four quadrants; the line y = x.
entries.problemDigest: Derives coordinate rules for reflection. A flag in the first quadrant is reflected over the y-axis and then the x-axis, and for each students list the image coordinates, write the rule, and say whether any points stay fixed — the points on the mirror line being the invariant ones. The What If section examines Kyrone's conjecture about reaching the third quadrant, which is where composing two reflections becomes equivalent to a single other transformation, and then has students reflect over the line y = x and write that rule, which swaps the coordinates rather than negating one. The closing question asks for all three rules together.
entries.approachGuidance: Kyrone's conjecture is for students to test and explain. Support their reasoning about why a composition behaves as it does.

entries.priorKnowledge: Rotations about a centre and the equal-distance, equal-angle relationship; coordinate rules for translations and reflections; plotting in four quadrants; that composing two transformations may equal a single one.
entries.problemDigest: Completes the set with coordinate rules for rotation. Students rotate a flag about one of its vertices, look for the relationship between the original coordinates and their images, and write the rule for each rotation — the quarter-turn rules swapping the coordinates and changing a sign, the half-turn negating both. The What If section returns to Kyrone, who revisits his earlier conjecture now that rotations are available, giving students a second pass at whether a composition of transformations can be replaced by one. The closing question asks for rules for 90° and 180° rotations and why each preserves size and shape.
entries.approachGuidance: Students derive the rules from the coordinates they generate. Support the pattern-finding rather than supplying the quarter-turn rule.

entries.priorKnowledge: The three congruence transformations and their coordinate rules; congruence by transformation; from Stretching and Shrinking, scale drawings, similar figures, scale factor and the rubber-band stretcher; ratios of corresponding sides.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces dilation as the transformation that changes size, reconnecting with the rubber-band stretcher. A dilation with scale factor 1.5 about a centre P carries one triangle to a similar one, and students describe how size and shape are affected, what happens to corresponding sides and angles, and what relationship holds among the centre, a vertex and its image — the three being collinear, with distances in the scale factor's ratio. The What If section reverses it, finding the centre and scale factor of unlabelled dilations, then examines Jamal's claim that the coordinate rules he used to enlarge Mug were dilations, including how the rule affects each point's distance from the origin.
entries.approachGuidance: Students describe what they notice about the dilation before it is formalised, and find centres themselves. Support their observations rather than stating the collinearity result.

entries.priorKnowledge: Dilation, centre of dilation and scale factor; congruence as a sequence of reflections, translations and rotations; that dilations preserve shape but not size; corresponding parts of similar figures.
entries.problemDigest: Extends the transformational definition from congruence to similarity. Two versions of a logo look similar, but no single dilation maps one onto the other because they are also turned or flipped relative to each other. Students work out what strategies would check similarity and which transformations would demonstrate it — the answer being a dilation combined with congruence transformations, so that similarity is defined as a sequence including exactly that. This is the counterpart of 2.1 for similarity, and the short problem turns on recognising that a dilation alone is not enough.
entries.approachGuidance: Several sequences will carry one logo onto the other. Support any sequence a student can justify rather than a preferred decomposition.

entries.priorKnowledge: Similarity as a dilation combined with congruence transformations; that similar figures have congruent corresponding angles and corresponding sides in the ratio of the scale factor; minimum conditions for triangle congruence from 2.2; measuring sides and angles.
entries.problemDigest: Asks the minimum-information question again, now for similarity. Students consider conjectures about how many pairs of corresponding sides or angles must be known before two triangles can be declared similar, and decide whether each line of reasoning holds — the parallel to 2.2 being deliberate, with measurement replacing the search for a sequence of transformations. The What If section applies similar triangles to indirect measurement, finding the height of a streetlight and a tree from a diagram, and then has students estimate the height of something too tall to measure using a mirror, so the method is used on their own object and their own data.
entries.approachGuidance: Students test proposed criteria and then measure something of their own choosing. Support the conjecture being tested and the measurements taken.

entries.priorKnowledge: All four transformations and their coordinate rules; congruence and similarity defined by sequences of transformations; that a composition of two transformations may be replaced by a single one; identifying a transformation from a figure and its image.
entries.problemDigest: Closes the unit with a game that pulls the transformations together. Students arrange shape cards into a network in which each card can be reached from the previous one by a transformation, then describe their strategies, compare their network with classmates' — which will differ, since many arrangements work — and look for places where two transformations in their chain could be replaced by one. The What If section returns to the opening diagram of Mug Wump images and asks which are congruent to Mug, which are similar, and how the original could be moved onto each, so the unit ends on the same figure it began with.
entries.approachGuidance: Networks differ between students by design and the comparison is the point. Support the arrangement a student built rather than a tidier one.

entries.priorKnowledge: The whole unit: reflections, translations, rotations and dilations, each defined by the relationship between a point, its image and a line, vector or centre; coordinate rules for all four; congruence and similarity as sequences of transformations; minimum conditions for triangle congruence and similarity; transformation arguments for parallel-line angles and the 180° triangle sum.
entries.problemDigest: The unit's Mathematical Reflections, one per investigation, each asking what students know about transformations and their effects on a figure. The expected ground accumulates: what each transformation preserves and what it changes; how each is determined by a point-to-image relationship and how to recover the line, vector or centre from a figure and its image; how congruence and similarity are defined by sequences of transformations rather than by matching measurements; the coordinate rules and why each keeps size and shape; the minimum information that guarantees congruence or similarity of triangles; and how transformations justify the parallel-line angle relationships and the triangle angle sum.

entries.priorKnowledge: Whatever has been covered when the exercises are assigned; the banks are organised by investigation and are normally used alongside the corresponding problems rather than after the whole unit.
entries.problemDigest: The unit's ACE question banks — Applications, Connections and Extensions — gathered as one item and grouped by investigation rather than taught as a problem. The banks follow the investigations: performing reflections, translations and rotations and recovering the mirror line, translation line or centre from a figure and its image; showing two figures congruent by giving a sequence of transformations and applying minimum conditions for triangle congruence; writing and applying coordinate rules for each transformation on a grid; and dilations, similarity by transformation, similar-triangle criteria and indirect measurement. This is the unit's largest item by a wide margin and is individual practice on content introduced elsewhere.
